CHANGING CONVERSATIONS
ABOUT STUDENT PERFORMANCE

The State of Student Growth
• The existence of annual student testing together with
unique student identifiers forms the foundation for the
calculation of student growth.
• Over the last decade, most states have begun
calculation of longitudinal student growth using large
scale state assessments.
• Analysis of student growth is controversial because of
how it is most often used: For teacher and school
evaluation.
• For example, the development of the current Hawaii
Growth Model involved the creation of a diagnostically
useful quantity that could be used (or not used) at a
later time for many purposes. 3

Why Student Growth?
If you care about student achievement, then you care about student growth.

• Where you are is a function of
where you started and how
quickly you ve travelled since.

• Student growth and student
attainment/achievement are
related in this way.
• Distance = Rate x Time
• Those who start behind tend to
stay behind and those that start
ahead tend to stay ahead.

Student Growth:
Introductory Concepts
• The concept of student growth isn’t as difficult to understand
and popular perception suggests.
• Calculations may be complicated but knowing how to
calculate student growth is not synonymous with
understanding student growth:
• The number π (pi=3.14159…) is difficult to calculate but is simple to
understand conceptually.
• Height and weight percentiles associated with children are difficult to
calculate but are simple to understand conceptually.
• Computational details are important but often obscure a
simple conceptual basis.

Student Growth:
Introductory Concepts

• There are 3 general approaches of
calculating student growth:
• Growth as an amount of change (i.e., gain).
• Growth as a norm/peer referenced
quantity.
• Growth as a criterion referenced/growth-
to-standard quantity.

Student Growth: Growth as an Amount of
Change
• Growth as an amount of change:
• What could be more simple?
• Like height or weight just calculate the amount of change.
• Requires a common, across grade reporting scale (which
Hawaii has since 2015/SBAC).
• Growth = Score Time 2 - Score Time 1
• Not as simple as it seems:
• Comparisons between students often lead to wrong
conclusions.
• Interpreting change requires context.

Student Growth:
Growth as a Norm/Peer Reference Quantity
Back to our question: Which high jumper improved more?

• Judy improved 2 inches.
• Anna improved 6 inches.
• An inch is an inch!
• But is an inch really
an inch?
• 2 inches for an elite
jumper is far more
remarkable than 6
inches for a novice.

Student Growth:
Growth as a Norm/Peer Reference Quantity

• This is analogous to height/weight measures for infants.
• Growth amounts are tricky to interpret and require context.
• Looking at the progress of individuals with similar starting points (i.e., peer based
comparison) is a way to acquire that context.

Student Growth:
Growth as a Norm/Peer Reference Quantity
• Like with infant height/weight charts, peers are children/students with
similar characteristics.
• For growth analyses using large scale assessments, peers are
students with (at least) the same scale score history on the same
tests.
• Currently, the Hawaii Student Growth Percentile Model (i.e., the SGP/
Colorado Growth Model) creates growth norms for all students using
regression (i.e., peer-based) analyses.
• Value added models often include demographic variables (e.g.,
ethnicity) are part of peer comparison.
• Value-tables consider students starting in the same achievement
level for comparison.

Student Growth:
Criterion-Referenced / Growth-to-Standard
• The standards used to examine growth are often the
state’s performance standards.
• Peer based analyses (e.g., SGP) are used in many states
as part of growth-to-standard analyses.
• Growth-to-standard analyses produce growth targets
determining whether a student’s growth is sufficient to
reach/maintain state standards.
• Absent norms, criterion-referenced growth produces
results similar to achievement indicating:
• Students that start behind tend to stay behind.
• Students that start ahead tend to stay ahead.

The Student Growth Percentile (SGP) Model
• Research on the SGP model began in 2007.
• Based upon work in Colorado, the norm-referenced model
was extended to include a criterion-referenced component.
• Work in other states incorporating the model into state
reporting and accountability systems occurred in subsequent
years and student growth became more common across state
assessment systems.
• The goal of the model is to create an individual level growth
metric that is informative to different stakeholders ranging
from parents to policy makers.

Student Growth:
Options for Small Sample Sizes
• Almost all current growth models use large
amounts of data to create “norms” against
which student growth is judged.

• Absent large amounts of data (>1,000
grade/content area), professional
judgment replaces large-scale data-based
norms.

Student Growth:
Options for Small Sample Sizes
• Value-tables can be used to monitor
progress of students between achievement
bands established for year-to-year
assessments.

• Some states (e.g., Alaska) use value-tables,
particularly with smaller scale assessments
for evaluating student growth for
accountability purposes.

Engaging Families and

questions.
• Different stakeholder groups ask different
questions.
• Parents are often simply concerned with how
their child is doing.
• To effectively engage parents and communities
in a productive conversation about student
learning (i.e. growth), what should be done?

Student Growth Models:
Engaging Families and
Communities
• A useful growth model should describe:
– What is? How much are students learning/
growing?
– What should be? How much would we like
students to grow/learn?
– What is reasonable? How much is it reasonable
to expect students to grow/learn?
• Most growth models do not provide a
student level metric. They provide a school
summary used for accountability purposes.

Conclusions & Recommendations
• Subtraction isn’t a growth model. A growth model
requires one consider where a student begins.
• Norms require large numbers of students. Smaller
numbers of students requires professional
judgment to decide what is ambitious yet
reasonable progress for a student.
• Precision and accuracy of results must be balanced
with utility: Precise and accurate enough for what
purpose.
• A student level metric is necessary to make student
growth models meaningful for families and
communities.
